title: Non-material culture
lead: Non-material culture is the second of the seven ideas, and it covers the side of a group’s way of life that you cannot touch.

p: Non-material culture consists of ideas and meanings, including language, beliefs, values and norms. These are learned through socialisation and can differ between groups.
In plain words, non-material culture is everything in a culture that you cannot hold, such as the words people use and the ideas they share.

writers.name: Functionalists
writers.says: argue that learning shared norms and meanings helps people participate in group life.

list: The different languages that families speak at a festival are shared meanings rather than physical objects.
The beliefs that families explain behind their celebrations are ideas, so they are non-material culture.
Greeting visitors and offering food are norms that children learn, so they are part of non-material culture.
Norms, values and beliefs are all examples of non-material culture.
The meaning of a thumbs-up emoji is shared and learned from other people, and it can differ between groups of users.
The Irish language is a set of words and meanings that a group shares and that children learn through socialisation.

p: Define the term: Non-material culture consists of ideas and meanings, including language, beliefs, values and norms. These are learned through socialisation and can differ between groups.
Item link: The languages and beliefs in the item are shared meanings rather than physical objects.

quote.t: At the festival, families speak different languages and explain beliefs behind their celebrations. Children learn when it is polite to greet visitors or offer food.
